activity_context.topic_title: Expressing Inhomogeneous ODEs as First-Order Systems

examples.knowledge_point: Writing an Inhomogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
examples.problem:
Consider the third-order differential equation

$$
y''' + t y' - 8 y = 1 - t^2,
$$

where $y = y(t).$ If

$$
{\begin{aligned}y={x}_{1}(t) \\ {y}^{′}={x}_{2}(t) \\ {y}^{″}={x}_{3}(t),\end{aligned}
$$

then the given differential equation can be rewritten as the matrix equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf f(t),$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070598/assets/2b3ba6edd838ee516ad902008726afbca516ab15892aad0f236c5a2270261985.png)
Determine the matrices $A$ and $\mathbf{f}(t).$
examples.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′} & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of $x_1, x_2$ and $x_3.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $(y'''),$ we obtain

$$
y''' = - t y' + 8 y + 1 - t^2.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
y''' = - t x_2 + 8 x_1 + 1 - t^2.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=8{x}_{1}-t{x}_{2}+1-{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf f(t)$ as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070598/assets/5a343acd288c1f6ddc72320b4eb17d9f24d3d41adebec579e70b9ff7ba17d0bb.png)

Therefore, we conclude that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070598/assets/dcb089aa64d2aeb959e6b33b03afecef75de96962a0468eb31b590ed6ecad6eb.png)

feedback.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}-{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y=2t
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},$ ${x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}={y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y+2t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}={x}_{3}-3{x}_{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+2t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+2t.
$$
